property_summary: For every caller address, calling airDrop once on the correct contract always increments that caller's tokenBalance by 20 and leaves the reentrancy lock unset so subsequent calls from any address can also succeed; the mutant that never resets the lock can permanently block further airDrop calls causing later tokenBalance reads to differ.

For any caller A and any other actor B, after A successfully calls airDrop once on the reference contract, a subsequent call to airDrop by B remains possible (so B.tokenBalance increases by 20); the mutant that leaves the reentrancy lock set can permanently block that subsequent call so B.tokenBalance does not increase.

Invariant: Calling airDrop from any caller never increases tokenBalance of any address that already had a non-zero balance in the correct contract (because of hasNoBalance); the mutant removes that guard so there exist inputs where an address with non-zero balance can be increased, violating the invariant.

For any caller address A and attacker address B, if A already has a non-zero tokenBalance then calling airDrop from A never changes tokenBalance of A under the reference (hasNoBalance); the mutant lacking hasNoBalance allows airDrop to increase an already-nonzero balance for some fuzzed addresses.

Reference contract C forbids any caller with a non-zero tokenBalance from successfully receiving more tokens via airDrop (hasNoBalance), so for every caller address A and any caller of airDrop the balance of A remains unchanged if it was non-zero before; the mutant removes hasNoBalance so there exist inputs (a caller A with preexisting non-zero balance that also satisfies supportsToken) for which airDrop increases A's tokenBalance, violating this rule.

For every caller A that is a contract whose supportsToken() returns the expected bytes32, if A already has a non-zero tokenBalance then calling airDrop from A must revert (reference enforces hasNoBalance); the mutant removes that guard so there exists a contract caller A with preexisting non-zero balance that can successfully call airDrop and increase its tokenBalance.

For every caller address A that is a contract returning the expected supportsToken() bytes32, if A has a non-zero tokenBalance before calling airDrop(), then in the reference C the call must revert (so tokenBalance[A] stays unchanged); the mutant removing hasNoBalance allows some such contract-callers with preexisting non-zero balances to succeed and increase their balance.

For any caller address, calling airDrop from an address whose Bank.supportsToken() returns keccak256("Nu Token") always increases that caller's tokenBalance by 20 (reference holds for all inputs); the mutant comparing against "Other Token" will reject such callers and thus fail to increase balance for some caller addresses.

For any caller address, the reference contract allows airDrop only when the caller's prior tokenBalance is exactly 0 and after a successful call that caller's tokenBalance increases by 20; the mutant inverts this precondition, so it will refuse first-time callers and permit only existing holders, causing divergence for some caller addresses (e.g., an address with zero prior balance).

For any caller address, if before calling airDrop the caller's tokenBalance is 0 then after calling airDrop the caller's tokenBalance equals 20; the mutant inverts the precondition and will refuse first-time callers, so it breaks this property for some addresses.

For any caller address with initial tokenBalance == 0, calling airDrop succeeds and results in that caller's tokenBalance becoming 20 in the reference; the mutant inverts the precondition and will reject such callers, so there exists an address for which balances diverge after airDrop.

For every caller address that currently has zero tokenBalance, calling airDrop succeeds and leaves that caller with tokenBalance == 20; the mutant inverting hasNoBalance (requires nonzero balance) will reject such zero-balance callers, so some caller exists where post-call tokenBalance differs.

For any caller (actor) that currently has zero tokenBalance, after calling airDrop the reference contract always increases their tokenBalance by 20 (so tokenBalance[actor] == 20), whereas the mutant that removed the balance update will leave tokenBalance[actor] == 0 for some admissible callers — the property checks that tokenBalance becomes 20 after airDrop.

For any caller address, consecutive successful airDrop calls from that same caller are permitted by the reference implementation (the nonReentrant lock is reset after the call), whereas the mutant that never resets the reentrancy lock prevents any subsequent airDrop from the same caller (second call will fail); the test fuzzes the caller and demonstrates this difference.

For any caller address, after a successful first airDrop by that caller the reference contract allows a subsequent airDrop (the reentrancy lock is reset), whereas the mutant that doesn't reset the lock prevents a second airDrop from the same caller (second call reverts).

For any caller address that initially has zero tokenBalance and that is a contract reporting support for the token name, after making one successful airDrop call the correct contract allows a second airDrop call from the same caller (lock resets) whereas the mutant that fails to reset _locked will make that second call revert (breaking this property).

For any caller contract that reports support for the token and starts with zero balance, two sequential airDrop calls (from that caller) both succeed on the reference because the reentrancy lock is reset after each call; the mutant that never resets the lock causes the second call to revert, breaking this rule.

For any caller contract that supports the token and starts with zero balance, performing airDrop exactly once will leave the _locked flag false in the reference (so a subsequent view-read of tokenBalance on the same caller reflects the increment and further calls are not permanently blocked), whereas the mutant that fails to reset the reentrancy lock causes the contract to become permanently locked and thus a second airDrop attempt will revert; we observe this by checking that a second airDrop call (wrapped in try/catch) succeeds on the reference for all admissible fuzzed caller addresses that are contracts supporting the token and have zero initial balance, but fails on the mutant for some such caller.

For any caller address, calling airDrop from an address with zero tokenBalance will always increase that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that relaxes hasNoBalance to <= 0 allows some non-zero-balance callers (due to unsigned wrap or crafted state) to also pass and thus can make post-call tokenBalance differ from the reference for some inputs.

For every caller address, if that caller's initial tokenBalance is 0 then after calling airDrop() their tokenBalance increases by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant relaxing hasNoBalance to <= 0 can allow non-zero (wrapped) balances to call and thus can make the post-call tokenBalance differ from the reference for some fuzzed initial balances.

For every caller address, if their initial tokenBalance is 0 then calling airDrop() succeeds and leaves their tokenBalance equal to 20; the mutant that changes hasNoBalance to require tokenBalance[msg.sender] <= 0 lets some non-zero (wrapped) balances pass and thus can produce a different post-call tokenBalance for some initial states.

For any caller address and any initial tokenBalance value >= 0, the reference contract C only allows airDrop() to run when tokenBalance[msg.sender] == 0 (so after a successful call the caller's tokenBalance becomes exactly 20); the mutant relaxing the check to <= 0 permits certain wrapped large balances (i.e. balances > 0 that underflow/wrap when manipulated or allow unintended callers) to also pass and thus can make post-call tokenBalance not equal to 20 for some fuzzed initial balances — the test fuzzes an initial balance and caller to expose that difference.

For every caller address and initial tokenBalance, the reference C only allows airDrop() to succeed when tokenBalance[caller] == 0 (so after a successful call that caller's tokenBalance == 20); the mutant relaxing the check to tokenBalance[caller] <= 0 can erroneously allow callers with large wrapped balances to pass and thus produce a different post-call tokenBalance for some initial balances.
